Bayer Analysts Split on Valuation Even as Drug Approvals and Guidance Lift Pile Up
sum: Deutsche Bank Research lifted its price target on Bayer to EUR 65 from EUR 60 on Tuesday, keeping a "Buy" rating on the German life-sciences group. The upgrade rests on higher earnings estimates tied to the strength of the pharmaceuticals division, alongside progress in bringing down debt and in the US litigation overhang.

The move leaves the stock trading in a gap between two very different views of its worth. Bayer closed Friday at EUR 56.66 — above Jefferies' EUR 48.50 target but comfortably below Deutsche Bank's new mark.

Jefferies reaffirmed its "Hold" rating and EUR 48.50 target the same day. Analyst Michael Leuchten had anticipated the US approval of Asundexian, and in his view the green light has sharply reduced the risk attached to Bayer's pharmaceutical pipeline — even if it isn't enough to shift his recommendation.

That approval covers Sunharbo, the brand under which Asundexian will be sold, for cutting the risk of further strokes in adults who have recently suffered a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack, in each case alongside antiplatelet therapy. Bayer has flagged the US market launch for mid-to-late November and describes Asundexian as the world's first approved factor XIa inhibitor.

Other analysts have been nudging their valuations higher as well. One firm raised its fair value and reiterated a buy recommendation, while two further houses had already lifted their targets on 4 November and likewise advised buying. The targets from these three houses sit between EUR 64 and EUR 66.

Fresh from the pipeline came a second regulatory win on 4 November, when China approved Sevabertinib as a first-line treatment for patients with advanced HER2-mutated non-small cell lung cancer — a clearance that explicitly covers use at the start of therapy.

The analyst revisions follow hard numbers. Bayer reported group revenue of EUR 10.1 billion for the third quarter of 2026 on 3 November, with EBITDA before special items reaching EUR 1.62 billion. Both figures rose year on year, according to the company, and the stronger pharmaceuticals unit contributed to an improved full-year outlook that Bayer had already announced.

sum: Bayer's U.S. regulatory milestone is moving into the commercial phase. The Food and Drug Administration approved Sunharbo, the brand name for asundexian, on November 9, 2026, and Bayer announced the decision on November 10. The company's release describes the drug as the first approved Factor XIa inhibitor in the United States.

Sunharbo is indicated with antiplatelet therapy for adults with a recent non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack. The recommended dose is 50 milligrams once daily. The approval gives Bayer a new product in secondary stroke prevention, an area where the company is seeking to strengthen its Pharmaceuticals business as established products mature.

The approval rests on the Phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE study, which randomized 12,327 patients after a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA. Ischemic stroke occurred in 6.2 percent of patients receiving Sunharbo and antiplatelet therapy, compared with 8.4 percent in the placebo and antiplatelet group. Bayer reported a hazard ratio of 0.74 and a P value below 0.0001.

The safety profile remains central to the commercial outlook. Major bleeding was similar between the treatment and placebo groups at 1.6 and 1.5 events per 100 person-years, respectively. Gastrointestinal bleeding was higher with Sunharbo at 2.7 versus 2.1 events per 100 patient-years, and Bayer also reported increased hepatic enzymes among treated patients.

Bayer expects shipments to begin in the United States in mid-to-late November, followed by availability for hospitals and pharmacies. The company is also seeking approvals in additional markets. As of November 2026, applications remained under review by the European Medicines Agency and Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, while China's National Medical Products Administration had approved asundexian on October 26.

Management presents the U.S. authorization as a first-in-class opportunity in cardiovascular medicine. The commercial execution will determine how quickly the regulatory success translates into revenue, with prescribing adoption, reimbursement and the safety profile likely to shape early demand. The company has not provided a revenue forecast for Sunharbo in the cited release.

sum: Bayer's SUNHARBO has cleared a major regulatory hurdle in the United States, opening a new commercial opportunity in cardiovascular medicine. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the 50-milligram asundexian tablet on November 9 for adults with a recent non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack, used in combination with antiplatelet therapy.

Bayer announced the approval in a release dated November 10. The company said SUNHARBO is the first Factor XIa inhibitor approved in the United States and described the once-daily medicine as a new approach to secondary stroke prevention. The Bayer release said shipments should begin in mid-to-late November, with hospitals and pharmacies expected to be able to order the medicine shortly afterward.

The approval rests on the Phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE study, which randomized 12,327 patients to SUNHARBO or placebo while both groups received antiplatelet therapy. Bayer reported that ischemic stroke occurred in 6.2% of patients taking SUNHARBO compared with 8.4% in the placebo group. That represented a 26% reduction, with a hazard ratio of 0.74 and a P value below 0.0001.

The safety profile remains relevant for investors assessing the drug's commercial potential. Major bleeding rates were similar at 1.6 and 1.5 events per 100 person-years for SUNHARBO and placebo, respectively. Gastrointestinal bleeding was more frequent with SUNHARBO, at 2.7 versus 2.1 events per 100 patient-years, while diarrhea was the most frequently reported adverse reaction above 3%.

Regulatory clearance removes a key development risk, but revenue will depend on prescribing decisions, payer access and the speed of the US rollout. Bayer's first commercial focus will be secondary prevention after qualifying strokes or high-risk TIAs; the FDA indication does not cover stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.

Sunharbo had already received approval in China on October 26. Bayer said applications remain under review by the European Medicines Agency and Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare. Further approvals could broaden the addressable market, but the timing and scope of those decisions remain ahead.

sum: Bayer's Pharmaceuticals division received U.S. approval for Sunharbo on November 9, 2026, and Bayer announced the decision on November 10. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized the 50-milligram asundexian tablet in combination with antiplatelet therapy for adults following a recent non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack.

Bayer said in its announcement that Sunharbo is the first approved Factor XIa inhibitor worldwide. The medicine is designed to inhibit Factor XIa, a protein involved in the blood coagulation pathway, while targeting clot formation associated with ischemic stroke.

The approval rests on the Phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE study, which randomized 12,327 participants internationally. Bayer said the trial demonstrated superiority in reducing ischemic stroke when asundexian was combined with antiplatelet therapy, compared with antiplatelet therapy alone.

Asundexian reduced ischemic stroke by 26 percent in patients who had suffered a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk TIA. Bayer also reported a similar rate of major bleeding under the ISTH classification between asundexian and placebo. The FDA approval therefore gives Bayer a commercial foothold in a new treatment class, although the label applies to a defined patient group and does not cover stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.

Bayer said Sunharbo has also been approved in China and that applications in additional markets are under review. The breadth and timing of those decisions will determine how quickly the new product can contribute to Pharmaceuticals revenue.

The drug adds a potential growth driver to Bayer's cardiovascular and cerebrovascular portfolio. Investors still need to weigh the opportunity against the company's broader execution demands, including the conversion of clinical differentiation into prescription uptake and reimbursement. The FDA decision is a regulatory milestone, not a forecast of sales or earnings.

Bayer stock traded at 56.88 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 10:10 CET on Wednesday, November 11, 0.35 percent below the Xetra close of Tuesday, November 10. The move provides the market context for the approval but does not establish a causal reaction to the regulatory decision.

sum: Bayer shares slipped 0.7% on Friday to close at €55.08, with profit-taking setting in after a strong run for the week. The retreat came as investors weighed a cautious note from Jefferies against a more bullish call from UBS, while the pending court approval of the Roundup settlement remained a live overhang.

The week's brokerage actions pointed in different directions. UBS raised its price target to €66 from €62 on Wednesday and kept its buy rating, with analyst Matthew Weston citing the strong momentum of the pharmaceuticals division and pointing to the planned breakup of rival Corteva. DZ Bank moved its fair value for Bayer to €64 from €60 on Thursday, also maintaining a "Buy" stance.

Jefferies took a more guarded line on Friday, lifting its target to €48.50 from €46 but sticking with "Hold." Analyst Michael Leuchten noted that his forecasts sit at the lower end of the company's own guidance range, and flagged the outstanding approval of the Roundup settlement as a key legal catalyst.

Bayer's third-quarter 2026 results, released Tuesday, showed group revenue of €10.1 billion, up 4.1% in nominal terms and 1.9% after adjusting for currency and portfolio effects. EBITDA before special items climbed 6.9% to €1.62 billion, driven chiefly by growth in Pharmaceuticals, while Crop Science and Consumer Health lagged. The bottom line was less flattering: Bayer posted a net loss of €0.7 billion.

On the strength of the pharma business, the company lifted its full-year guidance for EBITDA before special items to a range of €9.8 billion to €10.3 billion, up from the previous €9.6 billion to €10.1 billion. It also raised its expected pharma margin to 25–27% and guided free cash flow to between minus €1.5 billion and minus €0.5 billion. Net financial debt is projected at €28.0 billion to €29.0 billion by year-end.

On the agricultural side, Bayer reported the first US shipment of its pre-emergence herbicide Convintro for the 2027 season. The product, built on the active ingredient diflufenican, is aimed at giving corn and soybean growers another tool against herbicide-resistant weeds, and is intended for use across both crops.

sum: Bayer raised several 2026 targets after reporting stronger third-quarter operating performance on November 3, with Pharmaceuticals driving the improvement. The company said the division is entering a new growth cycle, while Crop Science and Consumer Health continue to face market pressures.

According to Bayer's November 3 release, group sales rose 4.1 percent year over year to 10.053 billion euros. Adjusted for currency and portfolio effects, sales increased 1.9 percent. EBITDA before special items advanced 6.9 percent to 1.615 billion euros, including a positive currency effect of 36 million euros.

Pharmaceuticals was the central growth engine. Reported division sales increased 8.0 percent to 4.680 billion euros and rose 6.4 percent on a currency- and portfolio-adjusted basis. EBITDA before special items climbed 23.6 percent to 1.292 billion euros, lifting the division margin by 3.5 percentage points to 27.6 percent.

Nubeqa and Kerendia led the advance, with currency- and portfolio-adjusted sales growth of 58.3 percent and 64.9 percent, respectively. Bayer said Nubeqa generated approximately one billion euros in quarterly sales, while Kerendia exceeded one billion euros over the 12 months ended September 30, 2026. Xarelto and Eylea continued to decline because of patent expiries, although Bayer said the pace of decline was slowing.

The other divisions were less supportive. Crop Science sales fell 2.4 percent on a currency- and portfolio-adjusted basis, while its adjusted EBITDA dropped 41.3 percent to 101 million euros in the seasonally small quarter. Consumer Health sales were broadly stable on the same basis, but adjusted EBITDA declined 4.4 percent to 347 million euros.

Bayer raised its Pharmaceuticals adjusted EBITDA margin target to 25 to 27 percent from 23 to 25 percent previously. Group EBITDA before special items is now expected at 9.8 to 10.3 billion euros on a currency-adjusted basis, compared with the former range of 9.6 to 10.1 billion euros.

The company also lifted its free cash flow target by one billion euros to negative 1.5 to negative 0.5 billion euros and lowered its expected year-end net financial debt range to 28.0 to 29.0 billion euros from 29.0 to 30.0 billion euros.

(Il Sole 24 Ore Radiocor) - Bayer is soaring on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, buoyed by an upward revision to its full-year profit forecasts, following better-than-expected quarterly results, albeit still in the red. Sales in the Pharmaceuticals sector (prescription medicines) rose by 8 per cent to €4.7 billion on a reported basis. The quarterly net loss narrowed to 672 million euros from a loss of 963 million euros last year and was affected by write-downs and legal costs. Excluding non-recurring items, EBITDA rose by 6.9 per cent to 1.6 billion euros.

sum: Bayer investors are heading into the November 3 third-quarter report with a paradox on their hands. The earnings bar has been lowered sharply over the past month, yet the company's legal overhang just produced its first genuinely encouraging courtroom signal since the US Supreme Court weighed in this summer.

Consensus now looks for earnings per share of €0.42 on revenue of €10.00 billion when the quarterly statement lands at 07:30 CET, ahead of the opening bell. The investor video call follows at 14:00 CET. What makes the setup unusual is the divergence inside those numbers: revenue estimates have barely budged, while EPS forecasts have been cut by 28.14% over the past 30 days. A stable top line, in other words, has not carried through to the bottom line.

Richard Vosser at JPMorgan reaffirmed an "Overweight" rating and a €61 price target on Friday, framing the defense verdict in Missouri as one more step toward containing the litigation. Jefferies took a cooler view the same day. Michael Leuchten kept a "Hold" and a €46 target, calling the first glyphosate trial win since the Supreme Court's June ruling encouraging but pointing to the same missing piece both analysts flagged: the judge has yet to sign off on the proposed settlement.

The verdict itself came in the case of Theresa Aretino et al., where a Missouri jury ruled unanimously for Monsanto, according to Bayer. Three plaintiffs had pursued claims of alleged product defects, misrepresentation and negligence. It marked the first glyphosate trial since the June Supreme Court decision, and dpa-AFX identified it as the concrete trigger for the share price move that followed. The stock was giving back 0.5% today.

Roughly 65,000 US Roundup claims remain outstanding. The proposed collective settlement provides for up to $7.25 billion spread over a maximum of 21 years. Final judicial approval is pending, which means that payment envelope cannot be treated as a resolved liability — and even a settlement drawn over two decades would not remove the importance of the operating business to Bayer's financial room to maneuver.
That matters because of the balance sheet. Net financial debt stood at €33.35 billion as of June 30, with the ratio of net debt to EBITDA at 3.2 times.

sum: Bayer shares closed Wednesday at €45.65, up 3.9%, as investors digested a pair of pharmaceutical announcements that arrived from two very different stages of the drug-development pipeline. One is a regulatory green light in China. The other is an interim readout from a late-stage prostate cancer trial. Both strengthen the medical case for the company. Neither, on its own, tells shareholders anything concrete about revenue or profit.
That gap between clinical evidence and commercial results is where the real debate now sits.

The interim results, released Saturday, come from the Phase III DASL-HiCaP study. According to Bayer, NUBEQA — whose active ingredient is darolutamide — cut the risk of metastases or death by 58% versus placebo. The median follow-up period was 3.8 years. The four-year metastasis-free survival rate came in at 95% for the NUBEQA arm against 88% for the comparison group. Bayer thus reported both a relative risk reduction and absolute survival rates at a fixed observation point — a more complete picture than a single headline number.

What the trial does not supply is any estimate of sales or earnings. A clinical endpoint of this kind establishes efficacy within the studied regimen. Translating that into a revenue line requires assumptions about uptake, pricing and reimbursement that the data themselves cannot settle.

Separately, China's regulator approved Asundexian under the brand name Sunharbo. The indication covers adults who have suffered a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk TIA, with the drug intended to lower the risk of further strokes. Bayer describes Asundexian as the world's first approved FXIa inhibitor — a genuine first-in-class milestone.

The two announcements should not be lumped together as equivalent wins. One is an interim analysis; the other is a granted marketing authorization in a specific territory for a specific patient population. They carry different evidentiary weight and different commercial timelines.

items.t: Bayer's Missouri Courtroom Test Looms Over a Year of Quiet Portfolio Surgery
sum: A fresh Roundup trial got underway this week in Missouri, and the timing could hardly be more delicate for Bayer. Three plaintiffs are taking on Monsanto, the group's US subsidiary, over allegations that the weedkiller was not adequately tested before it reached the market. Because the case is widely viewed as a bellwether for the glyphosate litigation still stacked up behind it, traders are watching closely — and they wasted little time reacting. Bayer shares shed 3.3% on the day the proceedings opened, closing at EUR 49.07.

The company rejects the claims. Its position is that glyphosate-based products are safe, and it has said it will keep cooperating with regulators as they revisit the science. That review is already moving: the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services have agreed to broaden their joint work on the ongoing glyphosate assessment.

What makes the Missouri hearing so consequential is that a proposed global settlement is already on the table. It would commit Bayer to payments of as much as USD 7.25 billion spread across 21 years. A hearing on that package was held roughly two weeks ago. If the judge declines to sign off, or sends it back for revisions, the company faces the prospect of years of individual trials with damage awards that are impossible to forecast.

That uncertainty remains the single biggest overhang for investors. Yet the equity has hardly behaved like a stock in distress. Since the start of the year it has gained 33%, and it currently trades at EUR 49.19. The 50-day moving average sits at EUR 48.61 — a level bulls would like to see hold.

While the courtroom drama plays out, management has been busy reshaping the balance sheet. On 21 September, Bayer agreed to sell the cancer drug Stivarga to Grünenthal in a deal worth up to EUR 375 million. Completion is targeted for late 2026 or early 2027. The logic is straightforward: free up cash, sharpen the pipeline's focus, and chip away at the debt pile left behind by the Monsanto acquisition.

Smaller disposals of this kind help at the margin, though they do not fundamentally alter the scale of the obligations. Investors are left weighing how quickly leverage can come down without starving the pharmaceutical business of the research spending it needs.

Bayer’s Supreme Court Win in Roundup Case No ‘Silver Bullet’
sum: After years of legal setbacks that have cost billions of dollars over its top-selling Roundup weedkiller, Bayer AG finally got a resounding win in the biggest tribunal of all.

The US Supreme Court threw out a jury verdict won by a Missouri man who blamed Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Backing Bayer’s appeal, the court said Thursday consumers can’t sue Bayer for the absence of a cancer warning on its label, given that federal regulators concluded a cautionary statement wasn’t necessary.

Bayer’s shares closed up nearly 19% Thursday, the most since 2003, as investors hailed a decision that could stem the tide of big-dollar verdicts, even if it doesn’t completely solve the company’s Roundup problem. They were down as much as 1.9% in early trading in Frankfurt on Friday.

“Finally common sense has prevailed as regulators, who are in tune with the technical and scientific issues, are in a better position to determine what is safe than juries,” said David Herro, a portfolio manager at Harris Associates, which is one of Bayer’s five biggest shareholders.

Litigation over Roundup had wiped out more than $60 billion in market value since Bayer inherited the world’s most widely-used weedkiller through its purchase of agrochemical producer Monsanto in 2018. Once an icon of German industry, Bayer has struggled to get a grip on the crisis through successive management regimes.

Problems with Bayer’s crop-science division have also weighed on the company’s ability to boost the performance of its other units, including the pharmaceutical business. Current Chief Executive Officer Bill Anderson’s turnaround plan has focused on resolving the conglomerate’s legal woes while also cutting bureaucracy.

The stakes are also high for Anderson personally. The American took the helm of Bayer in mid-2023, tasked with bringing a close to the protracted litigation that’s already cost the company more than $10 billion. He has vowed to largely contain the situation by the end of 2026. Shareholders made clear that his ability to succeed will weigh heavily on how they judge his future at the company.

items.t: Bayer Shares Surge 18% as U.S. Supreme Court Rejects Roundup Cancer Lawsuit, Lifting $10 Billion Litigation Cloud
sum: Bayer AG shares posted their biggest intraday gain in 23 years after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that consumers cannot sue the company for failing to include cancer risk warnings on its Roundup herbicide, providing a critical legal shield for the German pharmaceutical and agricultural giant.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled by a decisive 7-2 margin, overturning a jury verdict that had awarded $1.25 million (approximately NT$40 million) to a Missouri man who developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Following the announcement, Bayer's shares on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange surged more than 18% intraday, the largest such move since March 2003, with trading briefly halted due to extreme volatility.

The core dispute in this ruling centered on the boundary between federal and state law. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, writing for the majority, stated unequivocally that federal law requires uniformity in pesticide labeling. He argued that state-law claims based on a "failure to warn" would compel the addition of cancer warnings to Roundup labels, which would be "inconsistent with and outside the scope of" the labeling requirements approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

The legal basis for the case rests primarily on the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), which mandates compliant labels for pesticides while prohibiting states from imposing any additional requirements. Bayer argued that once the EPA approves a Roundup label without a cancer warning, the company faces no risk of being sued for the absence of such a warning.

In a statement following the ruling, Bayer said the decision "is a win for science, for farmers, and for the industries that rely on regulatory certainty to drive innovation," adding that it expects the ruling to lead to the dismissal of existing related lawsuits and effectively block similar future claims.

However, Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Neil Gorsuch dissented, voting against the majority opinion. Lawyers for plaintiff John Durnell argued that the EPA's determination should not prevent state courts from making independent judgments on the necessity of product warnings.

sum: The Trump administration yesterday handed Bayer another win, urging the Supreme Court in a new brief to side with the German pesticide company in a high-stakes legal case that could wipe out thousands of cancer lawsuits and potentially billions of dollars in liability tied to glyphosate-based Roundup weed killer.

Three out of nine U.S. officials who signed the brief previously worked for law firms that have represented Bayer, raising questions about whether the Trump administration is providing special favors and benefits to Bayer and siding with a foreign corporation against Americans with cancer.

The brief is the second Justice Department intervention in the case. In December, the DOJ asked the Court to review Bayer’s case. The court accepted the case in January and oral arguments are scheduled for April 27.

In the new filing, the Justice Department and Environmental Protection Agency urged the Court to rule in Bayer’s favor on the central legal issue: whether federal approval of a pesticide label under federal law preempts state failure-to-warn claims. If the Court accepts that argument, individuals would be barred from suing Bayer under state law for failing to warn that Roundup may cause cancer.

The salvo for Bayer is the latest in a series of favorable actions the Trump administration has provided to Bayer. On February 18, the White House invoked the Defense Production Act to guarantee supplies of glyphosate-based herbicides and elemental phosphorus, a raw element used in production of fertilizers, pesticides, herbicides, and a wide range of industrial and military chemicals. Regulators also reapproved dicamba, a Bayer herbicide twice blocked by federal courts, and cleared the way for new pesticides containing toxic, persistent PFAS “forever” chemicals.

We reviewed the company’s ties to the Trump administration and found numerous connections between Bayer’s lobby and legal firms and senior officials in decision-making positions affecting pesticides regulations, chemical safety, and how our nation’s food system is shaped. The new Supreme Court filing adds more Bayer ties.
Signers on the brief include Deputy Solicitor General Sarah M. Harris, who swung between roles at Trump’s Justice Departments and a law firm that represented Bayer in product liability cases.

Bayer’s $7 Billion Effort to End Roundup Curse Draws Skepticism
sum: Bayer AG Chief Executive Officer Bill Anderson’s effort to extricate the company from the years-long legal battles related to its Roundup pesticide is facing some skepticism from investors.

The German conglomerate’s proposed $7.25 billion class-action settlement in the U.S. announced late Tuesday to resolve most current and future claims that Roundup causes cancer — an allegation Bayer rejects but one that has haunted it since its $63 billion purchase of Monsanto in 2018 — initially sparked optimism.

But a cold-eyed look at the challenges the plan faces is prompting investors to pull back. After rallying 7.4% on Tuesday, shares reversed course, dropping as much as 12% on Wednesday, the steepest slide in over a year.
“This is not yet the breakthrough that many investors had hoped for,” said Markus Manns, portfolio manager at Frankfurt-based asset manager Union Investment, a Bayer investor.

The list of hurdles to the plan is long. For one, it remains contingent on court approval in Missouri. Class members can opt out, and Bayer has the right to terminate the agreement if participation falls short. Anderson has made clear the uptake needs to be “very close” to 100% participation for the framework to work.

The deal is also costly. Bayer raised its litigation provisions to €11.8 billion ($13.9 billion) and warned that free cash flow will likely be negative in 2026 as it fronts the largest payments. It has secured an $8 billion bridge loan facility to fund the upfront outflows and plans to refinance the debt through senior bonds and hybrid securities.

Anderson has a lot riding on the deal. The American took the helm of Bayer in mid-2023, tasked above all with finding a way to bring a close to the seemingly never-ending litigation that’s already cost the group north of $10 billion. He has vowed to largely contain the situation by the end of 2026 and is now arguing that the timing for a class-action solution is finally right. Bayer reached a point where plaintiff lawyers were willing to come to the table, he said, adding that the deal came after months of “difficult negotiations.”

items.t: Adrian Bayer: Unveiling the Universe’s Origins and Current State by Modeling Its Many Faces
sum: Just as cities, communities and people have histories, so too does the universe. The galaxies and stars we see today took shape over billions of years of cosmic evolution.

Using data science and machine learning, Adrian Bayer of the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Astrophysics (CCA) reconstructs the past, interprets the present and forecasts the future of the cosmos.

Bayer started as a research fellow this year at the CCA and is the co-leader of the Simons Observatory’s Sky Modeling working group. He holds a doctorate in physics from the University of California, Berkeley, a master’s in mathematics from the University of Cambridge and a bachelor’s in physics from Imperial College London. Before joining the CCA full-time, he worked as a postdoctoral researcher at Princeton University.
We recently discussed Bayer’s work and the value of learning from as many researchers as possible. This conversation has been edited for clarity.

In high school, I was very interested in how things work, particularly the inner workings of the human body and the structure of the universe. The body is at a very different scale than the universe, of course, but for me, understanding the dynamics of both was the key to understanding our place in the world.

Eventually, I had to choose between biology and physics. I arrived at physics, as it offered more opportunity to use mathematical and computational skills to solve problems, which I knew I would enjoy and find rewarding. I landed on cosmology after doing research in particle physics and quantum gravity because it’s a nice blend of theory and observation; as a cosmologist, I can apply the models and methods I develop to observations that are happening as we speak.

I use data science and machine learning techniques to understand how galaxies are distributed and formed throughout the universe. I also study the cosmic microwave background — a relic light from the early universe, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, now observed as microwave radiation that travels through space.

On one front, the Leverkusen-based conglomerate is pushing to expand the medical reach of its kidney drug Kerendia, filing a fresh application with China's National Medical Products Administration. On the other, the cost-cutting revolution engineered by CEO Bill Anderson is beginning to show up in the share price — and in the confidence of investors who once wouldn't touch the stock.

The submission to the Center for Drug Evaluation, a division of the NMPA, seeks approval for finerenon — marketed as Kerendia and Firialta — in adults with non-diabetic chronic kidney disease. That would mark a substantial broadening of the drug's current label, which already covers kidney disease tied to type-2 diabetes and specific forms of heart failure across more than 100 countries.

The application rests on data from the FIND-CKD Phase 3 trial, presented at the ERA congress in 2026 and subsequently published in the New England Journal of Medicine. The results showed finerenon significantly slowed the progression of kidney disease compared with placebo when added to standard therapy, while also reducing cardiovascular and renal events.

The potential patient pool is enormous. Roughly 850 million people worldwide live with chronic kidney disease, and in more than half of those cases, diabetes is not the underlying cause. Bayer points out that in advanced stages of the disease, the risk of kidney failure and cardiovascular events runs about 2.6 times higher than in the general population.

China is central to Bayer's pharma ambitions, and Kerendia is regarded as one of the most important assets in the company's pipeline — a candidate to offset revenue losses from older drugs facing patent expiries. Each additional indication and market brings that goal closer.

The stock's recent trajectory tells a story of its own. Bayer shares closed Friday at €48.49, up 5.48 percent over the week — a meaningful rebound after months of weakness. Year-to-date, the shares have gained 31.02 percent. A separate reading from the end of July put the price at €48.14, with a 12-month gain of 76.95 percent and a 30.07 percent advance since the start of the year.

items.t: Bayer files separate lawsuits against Moderna, J&J and Pfizer-BioNTech over COVID vaccine tech
sum: Bayer has filed separate lawsuits against the creators of three COVID-19 vaccines, claiming they violated intellectual property developed by Monsanto, the crop science company the German company acquired a decade ago.

In federal district court in Delaware, Bayer filed one complaint against Moderna and another against partners Pfizer and BioNTech. In U.S. district court in New Jersey, Bayer also is suing Johnson & Johnson.

The lawsuits allege that the defendants used Bayer’s technology in creating their vaccines “to eliminate ‘problem’ coding sequences in the building blocks of cells to improve mRNA stability and the amount or quality of protein produced.”
Pfizer and J&J did not respond to a request for comment. Moderna and BioNTech responded but only to say they were aware of the litigation.

Monsanto filed to protect its intellectual property in 1989, and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office eventually granted it in 2010, according to the lawsuits. Bayer bought out Monsanto for $66 billion in 2016.

Monsanto initially used the technology to increase the expression of an insect-resistant protein in crops, which reduced the need for pesticide sprays and improved agricultural output, the lawsuits explained.

Instability leading to poor protein expression was a central issue the COVID-19 vaccine makers faced in developing their shots. Solving this helped enhance the vaccines' “ability to confer immunity to the virus,” Bayer wrote in its complaint against Pfizer/BioNTech, adding that the German biotech has “acknowledged that it utilizes codon optimization in its mRNA products.”

items.t: Trump administration backs Bayer bid to limit Roundup lawsuits over glyphosate
sum: The administration of US President Donald Trump has backed German chemical firm Bayer in its bid to get the Supreme Court to shield it from liability over cancer claims related to its Roundup weedkiller, Reuters reported.
Bayer had paid about US$10bn to settle lawsuits linked to its glyphosate-based Roundup, which came with its US$63bn acquisition of agrochemical firm Monsanto in 2018, the 2 December report said.

In a brief filed at the Supreme Court, US Solicitor General D John Sauer said Bayer was correct that federal law governing pesticides pre-empted lawsuits making claims over products under state law, Reuters wrote.

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had repeatedly determined that glyphosate was not likely to be carcinogenic in humans and had repeatedly approved Roundup labels that did not contain cancer warnings, Sauer said in the brief.

"Where, as here, EPA has specified the health warnings that should appear on a particular pesticide’s label, a manufacturer should not be left subject” to state labelling regimes each prescribing different requirements, Sauer said.
“The labelling requirements imposed by Missouri’s failure-to-warn law are pre-empted by [the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act,]” the brief stated.
The specific case at issue was a claim from Missouri, where cancer patient John Durnell was awarded US$1.25M, The Hill wrote on 2 December.

sum: LONDON — European stocks ticked higher on Tuesday, with shares struggling to find momentum after a broad sell-off marked the first day of the new month.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 ended the trading session just above the flatline, with all major regional bourses in mixed territory.
Utilities stocks were among those seeing the biggest gains in Europe on Tuesday, with the index adding 0.3%. The sector is widely seen as a stable bet in times of market turbulence.
Winners in the index included wind energy giant Orsted, up 3%, and electric utilities firm EDP, which ended the session 1.7% higher.
Elsewhere, the FTSE 350 Banks index added 1.2%, after the Bank of England trimmed its estimate — for the first time in a decade — of how much capital banks operating in the U.K. need as a buffer.
The central bank also said all of the U.K.'s major banks had passed its stress tests, which simulates economic shocks and their potential impact on lenders.

"The results of the 2025 Bank Capital Stress Test indicate that the UK banking system would be able to continue to support the economy even if economic conditions turn out materially worse than expected," the Bank of England said in its report on the results.
